pos: n. pl. (Latin, colleges of piety: the small devotional meetings begun by Philipp Jakob Spener at Frankfurt in 1670, the seedbed of Pietism)
etymology: Latin collegium, an association or society, and pietas, piety, dutifulness.
biblical_def: The collegia pietatis were small gatherings that Philipp Jakob Spener began in his own house at Frankfurt in 1670, in which members of his congregation met twice a week to read Scripture, apply the Sunday sermon, pray, and examine their own lives. In Pia Desideria (1675) Spener proposed them as a general remedy for a Lutheran church he judged orthodox in confession and dead in practice, describing them as little churches within the church, ecclesiolae in ecclesia. The device spread across Germany and became the organising cell of the whole Pietist movement; the Moravian bands at Herrnhut and the Methodist class meeting are its descendants. Act 2:42 is the pattern appealed to, a people continuing stedfastly “in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines piety as reverence of the Supreme Being and obedience to his commands, and a conference as a meeting for consultation or instruction.
webster_full: PI'ETY, n. Piety in principle, is a compound of veneration or reverence of the Supreme Being and love of his character, or veneration accompanied with love; and piety in practice, is the exercise of these affections in obedience to his will.
CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of two or more persons for conversing or deliberating on some serious subject; a formal discourse.
EDIFICA'TION, n. Improvement and progress of the mind in knowledge, in morals, or in faith and holiness.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: A pastor's parlour meeting that became the cell structure of Pietism, Moravianism, and Methodism.
corruption_paragraphs: Spener's diagnosis was accurate and the dictionary grants it: a church can hold a sound confession and have a membership that never reads the Bible, never prays, and never examines itself, and the confession will not survive two generations of that. Deu 6:7 requires the word to be talked of in the house and by the way, which is a domestic and conversational duty no sermon discharges on a congregation's behalf, and Jas 1:27 measures religion by visiting the afflicted and keeping unspotted.

The corruption lies in the structure's tendency rather than its intention. A little church within the church easily becomes a church beside the church: the members who meet begin to regard the gathered meeting as the real body and the congregation as the formal one, and the eldership loses its oversight of what is taught. 1Co 14:40 requires order, and Act 2:42 puts the apostles' doctrine first in the list, before fellowship. The dictionary's judgment is that such meetings are lawful and useful under the elders' oversight and dangerous when they become a parallel authority, which is precisely what happened in parts of Germany within Spener's own lifetime.
roots_summary: Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly; koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Hebrew shanan (H8150), to teach diligently.
roots_lines: Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to sharpen, teach diligently; Deuteronomy 6:7.
usage: “the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — doctrine named first.
“thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7) — the domestic duty behind it.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — under the elders, or not at all.

pos: n. (the Bible press founded at Halle in 1710 by Carl Hildebrand von Canstein, the first Bible society)
etymology: From the surname Canstein, a Westphalian noble family; institute, from Latin institutum, a thing established.
biblical_def: The Canstein Bible Institute was established at Halle in 1710 by Baron Carl Hildebrand von Canstein in partnership with August Hermann Francke, and is reckoned the first Bible society in the world. Its innovation was mechanical and decisive: instead of resetting the type for each edition, Canstein kept the pages standing, so that a Bible could be reprinted at any time without the chief cost of printing it. The result was Scripture sold at a price a labourer could pay — a New Testament for a few pennies, a whole Bible for a fraction of the previous cost. The press issued some three million copies in the eighteenth century, supplied the Halle-Danish mission at Tranquebar and the Moravians, and became the model for the British and Foreign Bible Society nearly a century later. Isa 55:11 is the confidence it ran on, that God's word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stereotype as a plate of fixed metallic types, and a Bible as the sacred volume containing the revelations of God.
webster_full: STE'REOTYPE, n. Literally, a fixed metal type; a plate of fixed or solid metallic types for printing books.
BIBLE, n. THE BOOK, by way of eminence; the sacred volume, in which are contained the revelations of God, the principles of Christian faith and the rules of practice.
IM'PRESSION, n. The act of pressing one body on another; the edition of a book, or the whole number printed at once.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Psa 78:6
That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:
corruption_summary: A baron kept the type standing, and the Bible became something a labourer could buy.
corruption_paragraphs: The Canstein press is a useful corrective to the idea that doctrinal movements advance by argument alone. Pietism's most lasting effect on German Christianity may simply be that Francke and Canstein put Bibles into houses that had never owned one, at a price a weaver could meet. 2Ti 3:15 assumes a child who has known the holy scriptures from infancy, which presupposes a copy in the house, and Psa 78:6 sets the aim at “the generation to come” (Psa 78:6).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the cost of Scripture is a pastoral question. For most of church history the chief barrier between a believer and his Bible was price, and the men who attacked the price — Canstein with standing type, the Bible societies with subsidy, the translators with a vernacular — did more for ordinary piety than most preachers. Heb 4:12 says the word is quick and powerful; a Bible nobody can afford is a sword in an armoury.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), word; reyqam (H7387), void; Greek energes (G1756), powerful, effective.
usage: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — the press's working assumption.
“from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — which presupposes a copy.
“That the generation to come might know them” (Psa 78:6) — the aim of cheap Bibles.

pos: n. (Heinrich Plütschau, 1677–1752, with Ziegenbalg the first Protestant missionary to India)
etymology: German surname Plütschau, from a Mecklenburg place name; Heinrich, home-ruler.
biblical_def: Heinrich Plütschau was a Halle-trained Pomeranian who, with Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, was sent by Frederick IV of Denmark to the Danish settlement at Tranquebar on the Coromandel coast, landing in July 1706. They were the first Protestant missionaries to India. The Danish commandant imprisoned Ziegenbalg and both men were opposed by the local European community, who held that the conversion of Indians was no business of a trading post. Plütschau worked chiefly among the Portuguese-speaking population and in the organising and defence of the mission; he returned to Europe in 1711 and spent the next years answering, in print and before patrons, the objections raised against the whole enterprise, before settling to a pastorate in Mecklenburg. Rom 10:14 is the question the Tranquebar mission existed to answer, “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a being sent with certain powers, and a factory as a trading house in a foreign country.
webster_full: MIS'SION, n. A being sent or delegated by authority, with certain powers for transacting business; persons sent to propagate religion.
FAC'TORY, n. A house or place where factors reside, to transact business for their employers; a trading settlement in a distant country.
HEA'THEN, n. A pagan; a Gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Isa 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
corruption_summary: The first Protestant missionaries to India were opposed hardest by the Europeans already there.
corruption_paragraphs: The Tranquebar mission establishes the pattern that recurs in Grant's struggle with the East India Company a century later: the settled European interest in a trading post is the mission's first opponent, because preaching unsettles the arrangements by which the trade is conducted. Mat 28:19 commands the teaching of all nations and names no exception for commercial convenience, and Isa 49:6 gives the Servant “for a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Plütschau, though the practice of advocacy at home is now sometimes treated as the lesser part of missionary work. It is not. A mission with no one to answer its critics in Europe loses its funds and its candidates, and Plütschau's years of defending Tranquebar in Denmark and Germany are what kept Ziegenbalg supplied. Act 20:27 holds in that work too: nothing of the counsel of God to be shunned, including before patrons who would prefer a quieter account of what the money is doing.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; Hebrew 'or (H216), light; Greek ethnos (G1484), nation.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; Romans 10:14.
usage: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — Tranquebar, 1706.
“a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6) — the commission the factory resented.
“all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — including before patrons.

pos: n. (Leonhard Dober, 1706–1766, Moravian potter, with David Nitschmann the first Moravian missionary, later Chief Elder of the Unity)
etymology: German Leonhard, lion-strong; surname Dober, of uncertain origin, possibly from a Slavic root meaning good.
biblical_def: Leonhard Dober was a potter at Herrnhut when Count Zinzendorf brought back from Copenhagen in 1731 the account of Anthony Ulrich, a converted slave from St Thomas who had asked that someone be sent to preach to the enslaved there. Dober and David Nitschmann the carpenter offered themselves, were chosen by lot, and sailed in August 1732, the first Moravian missionaries and among the first Protestants to go out for the express purpose of evangelising the enslaved. They went with no salary and no promise of support, Dober expecting to keep himself by his trade. He worked in St Thomas until 1734, was recalled, and from 1741 to 1749 held the office of Chief Elder of the Unity, which he laid down and which the Moravians then declared vacant in favour of Christ Himself. Phm 1:16 is the relation his mission assumed, “a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lot as that by which the fate of a thing is determined, and a potter as one whose occupation is to make earthen vessels.
webster_full: LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance, hazard, fortune; but in strictness of language, is the determination of Providence.
POT'TER, n. One whose occupation is to make earthen vessels.
BROTH'ER, n. A human being, or a Christian, considered as a kinsman or an associate in the same family of God.
scriptures: Phm 1:16
Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
corruption_summary: A potter sailed to the sugar islands to preach to slaves, with no salary and a trade in his hands.
corruption_paragraphs: The Moravian missionary method is worth stating because it is so rarely imitated. Dober went out to support himself by his craft, to live among the people he had come to, and to stay; the model produced a mission to the West Indian slaves that was decades ahead of any other Protestant body and that the planters could not easily refuse, since the missionaries were artisans and not agitators. Mar 16:15 is the commission without qualification, to “preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).

The dictionary notes the limit of the Moravian witness here honestly. They preached to the enslaved as brethren and so denied in practice the premise of the system, which is what Phm 1:16 does; they did not, in those first decades, attack the institution itself, and Exo 21:16 was available to them. The Moravians' missionary reports nonetheless became part of the evidence the abolitionists used. Dober's laying down of the office of Chief Elder, and the Unity's decision to leave it to Christ, is a separate and striking act of ecclesiastical self-denial.
roots_summary: Greek agapetos (G27), beloved; ktisis (G2937), creature; Hebrew basar (H1319), to bring tidings.
usage: “a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16) — what he went to St Thomas assuming.
“preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — no qualification for the enslaved.
“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — the text they did not yet press.

pos: n. (David Nitschmann, 1696–1772, Moravian carpenter, first missionary with Dober and afterwards bishop of the Unity)
etymology: Hebrew David, beloved; German surname Nitschmann, from a diminutive of Nicholas.
biblical_def: David Nitschmann was one of the Moravian refugees from Moravia who settled at Herrnhut, a carpenter by trade, and in August 1732 he sailed with Leonhard Dober for St Thomas as one of the first two Moravian missionaries. Several men of the name served the Unity in the same generation, and the records are easily confused; this one was consecrated a bishop and spent his life travelling to the mission settlements — the West Indies, Georgia, Pennsylvania — as the Unity's travelling overseer and builder. He crossed the Atlantic many times, led the company that founded Savannah's Moravian settlement, and was aboard with the Moravian party whose conduct in a mid-Atlantic storm in 1736 made so deep an impression on John Wesley. Heb 13:13 describes the shape of his life, going forth “unto him without the camp” (Heb 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer, and an emigrant as one who removes from his own country to settle in another.
webster_full: BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director; applied to Christ.
EM'IGRANT, n. One who removes his habitation, or quits one country or region to settle in another.
CAR'PENTER, n. An artificer who works in timber; a framer and builder of houses, and of ships.
scriptures: Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
corruption_summary: A carpenter who crossed the Atlantic again and again, building settlements for other men's missions.
corruption_paragraphs: The Moravians sent artisans, and Nitschmann is the type: a man whose contribution to the missionary enterprise was that he could frame a house, lead a company, and be relied on to arrive. Rom 15:20 describes the apostolic ambition to preach where Christ was not named, “lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20), and the Moravian settlements in Georgia, Pennsylvania, and the islands were literal foundations laid in such places.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the standing of the tradesman in the mission. Act 1:8 sets the witness to the uttermost part of the earth and does not restrict the sending to the educated; the Moravian movement is the clearest Protestant case of a missionary force drawn from potters, carpenters, and weavers, and it reached further in fifty years than the established churches had in two centuries. The confusion in the records between the several David Nitschmanns is itself evidence of the kind of men they were: they did not write about themselves.
roots_summary: Greek parembole (G3925), a camp; themelios (G2310), foundation; martus (G3144), a witness.
usage: “unto him without the camp” (Heb 13:13) — the shape of forty years.
“lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20) — and he laid literal ones.
“unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8) — carried there by tradesmen.

pos: n. (August Gottlieb Spangenberg, 1704–1792, Moravian bishop, organiser of the American missions and author of Idea Fidei Fratrum)
etymology: Latin Augustus, venerable; German surname Spangenberg, from a Hessian place name, the clasp hill.
biblical_def: August Gottlieb Spangenberg was an assistant at Halle who was dismissed from the university in 1733 for his Moravian connections, joined Zinzendorf at Herrnhut, and became the Unity's chief administrator. He organised the Moravian settlements in Georgia and then in Pennsylvania, where he founded the economy at Bethlehem under which the whole community pooled its labour so that the missionaries could be sent out at no personal cost; he surveyed the Wachovia tract in North Carolina. After Zinzendorf's death in 1760 he led the Unity, retired its very large debts, and curbed the extravagances of the preceding decade. His Idea Fidei Fratrum (1779) is the Moravian church's doctrinal statement, christocentric and deliberately modest in its claims. Mat 25:21 is the commendation his sort of work is given, “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an economy as the management of domestic or public affairs with frugality, and a settlement as the act of settling, a colony or plantation.
webster_full: ECON'OMY, n. Primarily, the management, regulation and government of a family or the concerns of a household; hence, the management of pecuniary concerns with frugality.
SET'TLEMENT, n. The act of settling, or state of being settled; a colony recently established; a place or region newly peopled.
DOC'TRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; whatever is laid down as true by an instructor or master.
scriptures: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: He paid off the Unity's debts, curbed its excesses, and wrote down what it actually believed.
corruption_paragraphs: Spangenberg is the figure who kept the Moravian movement from dissolving. The 1740s had produced at Herrnhut a period of extravagant devotional language and practice that the Moravians themselves afterwards called the Sifting Time, together with debts on a scale that threatened the whole enterprise; Spangenberg retired the debts, restrained the excesses, and in the Idea Fidei Fratrum set out the Unity's doctrine in sober order. 1Co 14:40 and Tit 1:9 are both in view: order in practice, and holding fast the faithful word as it was taught.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a movement of great missionary energy still needs a confession and a ledger. Enthusiasm funds nothing and defines nothing, and the men who arrive afterwards to write both are commonly resented. Act 15:6 shows the elders coming together to settle a matter rather than leaving it to the prevailing mood. The Bethlehem economy is a separate study: a pooled community explicitly organised so that its members' labour supported missionaries abroad, which is the Sustentation Fund's principle applied a century earlier and more radically.
roots_summary: Greek pistos (G4103), faithful; taxis (G5010), order; antechomai (G472), to hold fast.
roots_lines: Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to set over, appoint; Matthew 25:21.
usage: “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21) — a ledger and a confession.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — after the Sifting Time.
“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — the Idea Fidei Fratrum.

pos: n. (David Zeisberger, 1721–1808, Moravian missionary to the Delaware Indians for sixty-two years)
etymology: Hebrew David, beloved; German surname Zeisberger, from a Moravian place name.
biblical_def: David Zeisberger was born in Moravia, raised at Herrnhut and in Georgia, and from 1745 until his death in 1808 worked among the Iroquois and then chiefly the Delaware, learning both tongues and compiling grammars, dictionaries, a spelling book, and translations of Scripture and hymns into Delaware. He founded a succession of Christian Indian towns — Friedenshutten, Schoenbrunn, Gnadenhutten, Goshen — and moved them repeatedly as the frontier wars overtook them. In March 1782 Pennsylvania militia murdered about ninety of his converts at Gnadenhutten, most of them women and children, who had gathered in their mission buildings and offered no resistance. Zeisberger led the survivors on years of forced wandering through Ohio, Michigan, and Canada. Heb 11:38 is the sentence the record requires, “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety, and a massacre as the murder of many persons with cruelty.
webster_full: GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
MAS'SACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty; the indiscriminate killing of human beings.
VOCAB'ULARY, n. A list or collection of the words of a language, arranged in alphabetical order and explained.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
corruption_summary: Sixty-two years, two languages reduced to writing, and ninety of his converts murdered in their own mission.
corruption_paragraphs: The Gnadenhutten massacre of March 1782 is named here plainly because the record is not in doubt and the perpetrators were nominal Christians of European descent. The Christian Delaware had taken a position of neutrality in the frontier war, had surrendered their arms, and were killed in their own buildings by militia from Pennsylvania after being assembled on a pretext. Mat 5:10 pronounces the blessing on those persecuted for righteousness' sake, and the corruption to name is the use of a Christian nation's name by men doing murder for land.

Zeisberger's own labour is the other half and it is the longer half: sixty-two years, the Delaware language reduced to writing so that a people could read Scripture in it, and town after town rebuilt after each displacement. Mar 16:15 sent him and Rev 14:13 is what the Moravians read over the graves, that the dead who die in the Lord rest from their labours “and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13). His Delaware grammars and dictionaries remain primary sources for the language.
usage: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — Gnadenhutten, March 1782.
“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — the converts' case.
“and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13) — the grammars outlived the towns.

pos: n. (Georg Schmidt, 1709–1785, Moravian, first missionary to South Africa)
etymology: German occupational surname Schmidt, a smith; Greek Georgios, a husbandman.
biblical_def: George Schmidt was a Moravian who had already spent six years in Bohemian and Austrian prisons for his faith when he was sent in 1737 to the Cape of Good Hope, the first missionary of any Protestant body to South Africa. He settled among the Khoikhoi in the valley afterwards called Genadendal, the valley of grace, learned the language, taught reading, and gathered a small company. When he baptized some of his converts the Dutch Reformed clergy at the Cape protested that he had no ordination recognised by their church, and the Company authorities withdrew his permission; he left in 1744 and spent the remaining forty-one years of his life in Europe praying for a work he was never allowed to return to. Moravians who reached the valley in 1792 found an aged woman keeping his Dutch New Testament, and the congregation was gathered again. Isa 55:11 is what the story illustrates, that the word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ordination as the act of setting apart to an office in the church, and to baptize as to administer the sacrament of baptism.
webster_full: ORDINA'TION, n. The act of conferring holy orders or sacerdotal power; the act of settling or establishing a minister over a church.
BAP'TIZE, v.t. To administer the sacrament of baptism to; to christen.
INTERDICT', v.t. To forbid; to prohibit; to debar; to forbid communion.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Act 8:36
And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?
Act 8:37
And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
corruption_summary: He was expelled from South Africa for baptizing his converts, and the New Testament he left behind was still in use fifty years later.
corruption_paragraphs: The grounds of Schmidt's expulsion are worth stating exactly, because they were ecclesiastical and not moral. Nobody alleged that his converts were unconverted or that his teaching was false; the objection was that a Moravian artisan had administered baptism without orders the Cape consistory would acknowledge. Act 8:36 and Act 8:37 are the passage he had on his side: the eunuch asks “what doth hinder me to be baptized?” (Act 8:36), and Philip's answer concerns faith, not the administrator's credentials.

The corruption to name is a settled church using its order to prevent a work it had not undertaken itself. The Cape establishment had made no serious attempt to evangelise the Khoikhoi and prevented the man who did. Mar 16:15 is the commission it was obstructing. The sequel is the part that should be remembered: a woman kept the book for half a century, read it to whoever would listen, and the congregation that the clergy had dispersed was found waiting when the Moravians returned. Isa 55:11 is not a sentiment but a mechanism.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), word; Greek koluo (G2967), to hinder; baptizo (G907), to baptize.
usage: “what doth hinder me to be baptized?” (Act 8:36) — the text he had on his side.
“If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” (Act 8:37) — faith, not credentials.
“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — one New Testament, fifty years.

pos: n. (Johannes von Watteville, 1718–1788, Moravian bishop and visitor of the missions, son-in-law of Zinzendorf)
etymology: Swiss noble surname von Watteville, from the Bernese estate of that name.
biblical_def: John de Watteville was born Johannes Michael Langguth, the son of a Thuringian pastor, came to Herrnhut as a youth, and was adopted by the Bernese Baron Friedrich von Watteville, whose name he took. He married Zinzendorf's daughter Benigna, was consecrated a bishop of the Unity in 1747, and spent his life travelling: to the West Indies, to Pennsylvania and the American settlements, to Switzerland, Holland, and the Baltic, visiting congregations and missions as an overseer. He was a leader of the Unity's educational work and was deeply involved in the devotional practice of the 1740s, for which he was afterwards criticised within his own church. His office is the Moravian attempt at the New Testament episkope understood as oversight by visitation rather than jurisdiction over a diocese. Act 20:28 names the charge, to take heed to “all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a visitation as the act of visiting for inspection or examination, and an overseer as one who superintends.
webster_full: VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting; a judicial visit or official inspection of a church, school or other institution, by a superintendent or authorized officer.
OVERSEE'R, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; an inspector.
EP'ISCOPACY, n. Government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government in which diocesan bishops are established.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: A Moravian bishop whose office was travel and oversight rather than a diocese.
corruption_paragraphs: The Moravian episcopate is an oddity worth understanding. It descends by consecration from the ancient Unity of the Brethren, but it was not reconstituted as a ruling order over territories; a Moravian bishop ordained, visited, and counselled, while the government of the Unity lay with its synods and boards. That arrangement comes closer to the New Testament usage than the diocesan model, since Act 20:28 and 1Pe 5:2 use overseer and elder of the same men and tie the office to a flock actually fed.

The dictionary holds the two New Testament offices, elder and deacon, with elder, bishop, and overseer as three names for one office, and it therefore does not grant the title bishop as a third order. What de Watteville's career shows is that the function of visitation is a real need: congregations and missions scattered over three continents require someone who has seen them. Heb 13:17 and Eph 4:11 together describe pastors who watch for souls, and a mission field without visitation gets neither watching nor correction.
roots_summary: Greek episkopos (G1985), overseer; poimaino (G4165), to feed, shepherd; episkopeo (G1983), to oversee.
roots_lines: Greek poimaino (G4165) — to feed, tend as a shepherd; Acts 20:28.
Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, take the oversight; 1 Peter 5:2.
Greek agrupneo (G69) — to watch, keep awake; Hebrews 13:17.
usage: “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28) — the charge, not a territory.
“taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint” (1Pe 5:2) — elder and overseer, one office.
“they watch for your souls” (Heb 13:17) — which requires having seen them.

pos: n. (the Nederlandsch Zendeling Genootschap, founded at Rotterdam in 1797, the first Dutch Protestant missionary society)
etymology: Dutch zendeling, one sent, a missionary, and genootschap, a society or association.
biblical_def: The Netherlands Missionary Society was founded at Rotterdam in December 1797, four years after William Carey sailed and in direct imitation of the English societies; its founders were Dutch Reformed ministers and laymen who had read the English reports and concluded that a church with an empire of trading settlements had been sending ships and not preachers for two centuries. It trained and sent its own candidates rather than relying on volunteers, and its men went chiefly to the Dutch East Indies, to Java and the eastern islands, and to South Africa, where Johannes van der Kemp became its best-known agent among the Khoikhoi and the Xhosa. Karl Gützlaff, afterwards of China, was among those it trained. Rom 15:20 is the ambition it was founded on, to preach “not where Christ was named” (Rom 15:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a society as a number of persons united for some common object, and a seminary as a place of education.
webster_full: SOCI'ETY, n. A number of persons associated, either for mutual benefit, or for some common object; a company.
MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; one sent on a mission.
COL'ONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
scriptures: Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
Psa 67:2
That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.
And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: A trading empire of two centuries that had sent ships everywhere and preachers almost nowhere, corrected in 1797.
corruption_paragraphs: The founding of the society is an indictment of what preceded it. The Dutch Republic had held settlements from the Cape to the Moluccas since the early seventeenth century, with chaplains for its own people and almost no sustained effort to evangelise the populations among whom they traded; the Cape consistory's treatment of George Schmidt in 1744 is the same disposition in miniature. Mat 24:14 says the gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world “for a witness unto all nations” (Mat 24:14), and a chaplaincy to the factory is not that.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the society itself, though the whole era of missions under colonial administration is now commonly read as one undifferentiated enterprise. The distinction the dictionary insists on is the one this society's own founding makes: the trading company and the missionary society were different bodies with different aims, and the second was founded in reproach of the first. Psa 67:2 and Act 1:8 set the object; Rom 15:20 set the frontier.
roots_summary: Greek philotimeomai (G5389), to strive, make it one's ambition; marturion (G3142), a witness; Hebrew yeshu'ah (H3444), salvation.
roots_lines: Greek philotimeomai (G5389) — to strive earnestly, be ambitious; Romans 15:20.
usage: “not where Christ was named” (Rom 15:20) — the frontier it was founded for.
“for a witness unto all nations” (Mat 24:14) — which a factory chaplaincy is not.
“thy saving health among all nations” (Psa 67:2) — the object, two centuries late.
